Cloud security · Encryption · Data governance

When the Cloud Gets a Subpoena
Who Holds Your Keys?

Protecting sensitive cloud data with defense in depth, Bring Your Own Key, and Hold Your Own Key.

Understand the requestCompare BYOK and HYOKPlan your responseThree next steps

For chief security officers, government requests for cloud data raise an increasingly practical question: how much control does your organization retain when a third party holds its sensitive information?

A Wall Street Journal clipping titled “Tech Giants Resist ICE Requests,” identified as October 30, 2026, describes technology companies challenging or delaying some requests they considered overbroad, revisiting user notifications, and facing a growing volume of demands. It reports that Google received a record of about 28,600 U.S. government subpoenas between January and June 2025. That figure refers to subpoenas, not exclusively ICE requests and not all government data requests. [1]

The reporting is a useful starting point for a broader cloud security discussion. Provider review processes matter, but organizations also need to understand the technical controls over their own data. This blog focuses on two options—Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) and Hold Your Own Key (HYOK)—and how they fit into a defense in depth strategy.

The central distinction

BYOK gives you control over the origin and lifecycle of keys imported into a cloud service. HYOK can keep essential key material outside that provider’s infrastructure. Neither removes legal obligations, and neither automatically protects every copy of your data.

First, understand the request

“Subpoena” and “search warrant” are not interchangeable. The authority behind a request, the information sought, and the applicable law determine what a provider may disclose. The comparison below focuses on ordinary U.S. government requests for stored cloud information; civil discovery, national security authorities, emergencies, and other jurisdictions require separate analysis.

Common forms of U.S. legal process
RequestWho issues or authorizes it?Why the distinction matters
Administrative subpoenaAn agency acting under a specific statutory authority, generally without advance judicial approval.Its reach depends on that authority. Under the Stored Communications Act, an authorized subpoena can compel specified basic subscriber records; it is not a general warrant to obtain stored message content. Court review may follow a challenge or enforcement action. [2–3]
Grand jury subpoenaIssued through court process for a grand jury investigation, often at a prosecutor’s request; generally without a judge first finding probable cause for each subpoena.Can compel testimony or production within legal limits. A recipient can seek to quash or modify an unreasonable or oppressive document subpoena. It does not become a content search warrant simply because a grand jury is involved. [2,4]
Judicial search warrantA judge or magistrate judge, based on probable cause and the required supporting showing.Specifies the search or disclosure authorized. Google states that it requires a search warrant to compel stored communications content in U.S. criminal cases. [5] Google policy
Section 2703(d) court orderA court, under the Stored Communications Act.Requires specific and articulable facts meeting the statute’s relevance standard. It can reach certain non-content records beyond basic subscriber details, subject to constitutional and other legal limits. [2]

Preservation is a separate step. A government preservation request under 18 U.S.C. § 2703(f) requires a covered provider to preserve existing evidence pending legal process. It does not itself authorize disclosure. [2]

Who receives the request first?

There is no universal sequence. Authorities may serve the provider, the customer organization, or both. If the provider is served first, customer notice depends on the law, the request, contractual commitments, and provider policy. Notice may be prohibited or delayed, so your organization may learn of a request only after disclosure.

Published approaches illustrate the differences. Google describes legal review and user notification, including exceptions. AWS says it makes reasonable efforts to redirect enterprise content requests to customers, notifies them when legally permitted, and challenges inappropriate demands. Oracle describes case-by-case legal review, challenges to invalid requests, and notification safeguards subject to legal restrictions. The supplied WSJ clipping reports pushback by Meta and Google on particular demands; it does not establish an identical policy for every provider. [1]

Social media account requests and requests for enterprise cloud workloads also concern different services and data. A request for an account’s identity or IP history may involve records that your workload encryption does not protect.

Shared responsibility still applies

The shared responsibility model has long defined the division of security work between cloud providers and customers. Providers secure the underlying infrastructure. Customers remain responsible for their data, identities, access decisions, and the configurations they control. The precise boundary changes between infrastructure, platform, and software services. AWS and Microsoft explain these service-dependent responsibilities.

You still need defense in depth: endpoint protection, network security controls where applicable, secure coding, least privilege, and comprehensive logging, reporting, and alerting. Key control adds another layer to that foundation.

Protecting your data by controlling the keys

BYOK and HYOK offer different levels of control. The following diagram from the draft places them among several cloud data protection approaches. The arrows illustrate where control moves; the operational question is where the key material resides and which systems can authorize its use.

Bring Your Own Key

With BYOK, customers generate encryption key material and import it into a provider’s key management service. This provides greater control over key provenance and lifecycle than relying only on provider-generated keys. The imported copy operates within the cloud service’s security and authorization model; importing a key does not mean ordinary cloud administrators can simply read or export it. AWS KMS import FAQ

Managing a handful of keys manually may be feasible. Across multiple clouds, regions, applications, and key versions, it becomes harder to track ownership, rotation, expiration, and the mapping between source keys and cloud keys. Centralized management can improve visibility and reduce administrative effort.

Hold Your Own Key

HYOK keeps essential key material in an external key manager, potentially backed by a hardware security module, under your organization’s control. Supported cloud services request cryptographic operations through an integration rather than importing that external key material into the provider’s native keystore. AWS XKS and Google Cloud EKM document this approach.

The benefits include separation of key custody from data hosting, independent authorization controls, and additional evidence about key use. These controls can support regulatory and contractual requirements when the implementation meets those requirements. They do not create a blanket compliance guarantee.

HYOK is not appropriate for every workload. Classify data according to sensitivity, business impact, and processing needs. Less sensitive data may be adequately protected by native controls; highly sensitive data may justify external key custody and its operational cost. In Microsoft environments, sensitivity labels, access controls, retention, and audit policies remain part of that decision.

External key custody has a boundary

Cloud services may still process plaintext after authorized decryption. Existing plaintext, cached data keys, exports, backups under other keys, and subscriber metadata can remain accessible. Protecting data during processing requires additional controls beyond key custody.

When a request arrives

The BYOK scenario

An organization uses Thales CipherTrust Cloud Key Management (CCKM) to manage a key imported into AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or Google Cloud KMS. It then disables a key in its own environment. Does that prevent the cloud provider from decrypting the data?

Disabling a cloud encryption key should prevent new operations that require it, according to the service’s documented behavior. Confirm the resulting cloud state and test the affected workload. AWS, for example, distinguishes imported material, the KMS key, and their lifecycle controls. AWS KMS FAQ

That still does not prove that all data is inaccessible. Previously decrypted information or cached data keys may remain usable. AWS explicitly documents caching exceptions for integrated services. A legal demand does not establish a universal technical bypass of disabled keys; equally, a disabled key does not establish that the provider possesses no responsive information. AWS guidance on external key revocation

The HYOK scenario

With an external key integration, the essential external wrapping key remains in CipherTrust Manager or a supported HSM rather than being imported into the cloud keystore. For operations that require it, the external manager can enforce authorization before returning a cryptographic result. CCKM supplies management and integration capabilities; key custody depends on the configured deployment. Thales CCKM overview

If the required external operation is denied, a new decryption that depends on it cannot complete through that path. This is a meaningful control over access, subject to cached keys, plaintext copies, workload behavior, and other access paths. It does not make access impossible in every circumstance, and authorities may direct valid legal process to the organization or another key custodian.

A coordinated response workflow

  1. Route and authenticate. Send any request or provider notice to legal counsel and the designated security response owner. Verify the source, authority, scope, deadlines, and any notification restrictions.
  2. Preserve and assess. Under counsel’s direction, preserve responsive data, logs, and relevant key state. Map the requested information to applications, regions, key versions, caches, and custodians.
  3. Review the available response. Counsel evaluates compliance, clarification, narrowing, or a challenge. Security documents what the provider and customer can technically access and coordinates with the provider when permitted.
  4. Execute and document. Carry out the approved response with an audit trail. Do not disable or destroy keys to frustrate a legal request; key changes affecting preserved information require legal review.

What about antitrust pressure and AI?

The clipping reports concerns among Google executives about government retaliation while the company faced antitrust cases. That is attributed reporting about particular concerns, not evidence that every provider will relax its standards. [1]

Useful procurement questions are more concrete: who approves disclosures, how are overbroad requests challenged, when is customer notice withheld, and what audit evidence is retained? If automation assists triage, ask how accountable legal review and exception handling are maintained.

How external key control works in practice

AWS KMS External Key Store

AWS XKS connects AWS KMS to a customer-controlled external key manager through an XKS proxy. AWS documents a double encryption design that uses both AWS KMS material and external key material. The diagram below shows the architecture; the steps describe an envelope encryption flow for a supported integrated service. AWS XKS cryptographic operations

  1. An application uploads an object to a supported AWS service configured to use an XKS-backed KMS key.
  2. The service requests a data key from AWS KMS. KMS generates the data key and encrypts a copy using its own key material.
  3. KMS sends that encrypted copy through the XKS proxy for a second encryption operation using the external key. The proxy and external system enforce the configured authentication and authorization controls.
  4. The external system returns the doubly encrypted data key. The external key material stays outside AWS.
  5. KMS returns the plaintext data key and its encrypted copy to the service. The service uses the plaintext key to encrypt the object and stores the encrypted key with the protected data.
  6. A later decryption requires the corresponding unwrapping operations, unless the service can use an existing cached data key. Check service-specific caching and key handling behavior.

The external system becomes an availability dependency. Design and test its network path, authentication, capacity, monitoring, failover, and recovery. AWS external key store considerations

Google Cloud External Key Manager

Google Cloud EKM integrates Cloud KMS with a supported external key manager. External key material is never sent to Google. For supported services, access to protected data depends on the necessary external cryptographic operation. Cloud EKM overview

Where supported and configured, Key Access Justifications adds a reason code to key access requests. An external policy can use that code to approve or deny an operation. Evaluate the supported services, coverage, and policy behavior for your deployment. A justification code is a technical policy input; it is not a substitute for legal review. Key Access Justifications

Microsoft Purview Double Key Encryption

Microsoft DKE protects supported content with two keys: one controlled by the organization and one held through Microsoft’s services. Both are required for access. This is a content protection approach for supported applications, rather than a general external keystore for every Azure workload. Microsoft documents limitations for online viewing and cloud capabilities that require content access. Validate those tradeoffs before selecting DKE for highly sensitive documents. Microsoft DKE documentation

Three things organizations can do next

  • Classify and map sensitive data. Identify the workloads that need independent key control, then map data copies, metadata, key versions, and decryption paths across providers.
  • Pilot and verify the controls. Compare BYOK and HYOK on a representative workload. Test actual key disablement, cache behavior, availability failures, restoration, and the evidence captured in cloud and external key logs.
  • Rehearse the legal response. Establish owners across legal, security, privacy, and operations. Confirm provider notification commitments and run a tabletop exercise that includes a preservation demand and a request received without advance customer notice.

Control begins before the request

The WSJ reporting highlights the pressure created by growing request volumes, disputed scope, and notification decisions. Organizations cannot base a sensitive data strategy solely on how a provider might respond to a future demand.

BYOK can improve key lifecycle control and visibility. HYOK can add independent custody and authorization over essential key material. The right choice depends on the data, service capabilities, processing requirements, and the organization’s ability to operate the external infrastructure reliably.

The goal is a clear, tested understanding of who can access your information, under what conditions, and with what evidence. Combine that understanding with defense in depth and a coordinated legal response, and your organization will be better prepared when a request arrives.
